This paper presents a systematic empirical comparison of five LLM augmentation strategies applied to document-grounded question answering over a corpus of academic research documents: (1) Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with FAISS vector search and bibliography filtering, (2) Knowledge Graph (KG) augmentation using NetworkX-based co-occurrence graphs, (3) a Multi-Step Reasoning Agent employing iterative plan-searchreason-synthesise cycles, (4) parameter-efficient fine-tuning of TinyLlama-1.1B via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), and (5) a Hybrid approach combining all three retrieval strategies to feed the fine-tuned model. Using TinyLlama\/TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 as the base model across all conditions, we evaluate each approach on five domain-relevant research questions using keyword-overlap relevance scoring and response-time measurement. The Multi-Step Agent achieved the highest average relevance score (0.88), followed by the Hybrid approach (0.67) and Fine-tuning (0.46), while vanilla RAG performed the worst on direct relevance despite lower latency. Our analysis identifies trade-offs between answer quality, computational cost, and deployment complexity, yielding practical guidance for researchers and practitioners selecting LLM augmentation strategies for knowledge-intensive
